Small banks say they're on top of risk
TEXT:
Regional bank bosses have assured a parliamentary committee they've got zero tolerance for breaches of anti-money laundering laws and are not aware of any problems that would expose them to the sort of action AUSTRAC launched against Westpac.

Bank of Queensland CEO George Frazis said the bank had a well-funded project to improve its anti-money laundering controls, including automating manual processes, in response to AUSTRAC identifying "potential compliance contraventions" after a review last year. "This is not about not being compliant with our reporting obligations, this is about strengthening our systems and processes," he said.

"We are comfortable about the robustness of our processes around AML [anti-money laundering]."

Bendigo and Adelaide Bank CEO Marnie Baker said after Westpac originally identified its issues reporting international transfers, Bendigo reviewed its processes and is doing another review now. She said the bank was confident its systems work properly. "We don't use the same systems as Westpac does," she said. "We have participated with AUSTRAC ... they haven't raised any concerns with us."

Macquarie's banking boss, Greg Ward, told the House of Representatives standing committee on economics the bank makes 4000 international fund transfer instructions reports a month - a relatively small number compared with the big four - and confirmed it has no outstanding issues with AUSTRAC.

After a week when Westpac CEO Brian Hartzer stepped down after failures in the bank's risk management systems were exposed, Australian Banking Association chief Anna Bligh said on Friday: "I would expect every bank is right now, and has been for some time, looking at the resources they are allocating, their systems ... [and] the appropriate application of accountability."

Mr Frazis also sought to distinguish BoQ from his former employer - he previously ran Westpac's retail bank - saying BoQ only uses the SWIFT messaging system when making international money transfers.

It was Westpac's use of non-SWIFT payment messages that tripped it up with AUSTRAC because instructions in the non-SWIFT payments didn't contain enough information to satisfy its legal obligations.

"All of our international transfers go through the SWIFT gateway," Mr Frazis said. "There is no innovative product left outside that ... that we provide."

The smaller banks also used the hearings in Canberra on Friday to reiterate their long-held desire for policymakers to close the gap between the amount of capital they need to hold, and the lower amounts required of big banks, which reduces the majors' funding costs.

Overall, the small banks say the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA) requires them to hold 50 per cent more capital than the majors and Mr Frazis said it was "perverse" the big four can compete much more aggressively for low-risk loans. He said the major banks also receive a 15 to 20 basis point funding cost advantage due to the perception they are "too big to fail" and will be bailed out by taxpayers if they were on the verge of collapse.

"The political reality is [a regional bank] would not be allowed to fail'," said Ms Bligh, adding this supported arguments for policies that help reduce small bank-funding costs.

Meanwhile, Macquarie revealed the extent to which it is taking on the major banks in the core area of mortgages.

Macquarie has a 2.3 per cent share of the overall mortgage market, but Mr Ward said the bank's current share of new mortgages being written by brokers was 12 per cent. Fast approval times are key, after the big four tripped on origination processes after the royal commission and scrutiny of "responsible lending" obligations.

"We are growing very fast - we are the best in the market for turnaround time for mortgage approval," he said.

HEADLINE: 'Double standard': dirty-money laws lag
TEXT:
The Morrison government's failure to tighten anti-money-laundering laws has allowed billions of dollars each year handled by lawyers, accountants and real estate agents to potentially fund terrorism, drug trafficking and child exploitation.

Prime Minister Scott Morrision and his senior ministers have spent the week excoriating Westpac for its breaches of anti-money-laundering laws, criticism labelled hypocritical as the government drags its feet on implementing tougher rules.

Australia is ranked alongside Haiti and Madagascar for its lax anti-money-laundering rules, a result that led a global taskforce to suspend a review of Canberra's performance last month.

"You can't have Scott Morrison and [Home Affairs Minister] Peter Dutton lambasting Westpac while they've done nothing around anti-money-laundering and compliance," said Grant Halvorsen, a payments expert with more than 30 years' experience in the industry.

"It's double standards. Australia is lagging badly."

The main issue is Australia's failure to enact the so called "tranche 2" anti-money-laundering laws, which would compel real estate agents, lawyers and accountants to report suspicious transactions. The proposed laws have been resisted fiercely by the real estate sector and law firms, leading to a 13-year delay in delivering a tougher compliance regime.

The real estate sector has often been identified as a large compliance hole, with financial intelligence agency AUSTRAC estimating $1 billion in suspicious transactions came into the Australian property market from China in the 2016 financial year.

AFR Weekend has been told that by Christmas the federal government will receive a submission from the Department of Home Affairs outlining options to toughen Australia's anti-money-laundering regime.

However, in recent statements Home Affairs has indicated that although it is "committed to continually improving Australia's anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism financing laws", it is worried about "placing undue burden on industry".

Another government source said there were concerns any tougher rules would be seen as "re-regulation" or adding more "red tape".

Labor member Daniel Mulino said the government had to explain its plans to tighten money-laundering laws.

"We know the Morrison government has dragged their heels on anti-money-laundering and counter-terrorism financing reforms," said Dr Mulino, a member of the House of Representatives economics committee.

"It's right that Westpac is being held to account for their shocking failings, but we shouldn't ignore the fact that the Morrison government's failure to act is leaving Australia exposed as a weak link.

The Australian Financial Review has highlighted glaring weaknesses in Australia's anti-money-laundering regime over recent weeks in its Huang Files series.

It revealed that a 32-year-old Chinese-born man, Zhang Bo, had six houses in Sydney's Mosman worth $37 million, but lived in none of them.

The Financial Review also revealed that political fixer Sevag Chalabian used the bank account of his 81-year-old mother to receive an $11 million payment associated with the purchase of a commercial property by Huang Xiangmo's Yuhu Group.

Tougher anti-money-laundering laws may have forced those involved in these transactions to flag them with authorities.

Over the past five years, as Australia has baulked at introducing stricter compliance, New Zealand has implemented tranches 1 and 2 of the anti-money-laundering laws.

In parliament on Monday, Mr Dutton used question time to say Westpac's bosses had "given a free pass to paedophiles" and should pay the price.

Westpac has been accused by AUSTRAC of 23 million breaches of the laws, including failing to notify the regulator of suspicious transactions by people involved in child exploitation.

Mr Morrison was equally critical of Westpac and indicated he felt senior management and members of the board should consider standing aside.

Another weak spot in regulation is in the emerging area of digital currencies, where authorities struggle to stay ahead of the options available for those looking to send virtual money around the globe.

Figures released on Thursday by US-based crypto-intelligence firm CipherTrace found that two-thirds of the world's top 120 digital currency exchanges had weak Know Your Customer (KYC) policies, and $US4.4 billion ($6.5 billion) had been attributed to cryptocurrency-related frauds and thefts so far this year.

Digital currency exchanges have fallen under the authority of AUSTRAC since April 2018, but Australian cyber-security expert Troy Hunt said it was still notoriously easy for crooks to remain anonymous.

"Exchanges tend to be a little more formal , but there are plenty of other services where you can convert cryptocurrency back into cash, which don't undergo the same regulation," he said.

CipherTrace chief executive Dave Jevans said new global Financial Action Task Force (FATF) guidance on policing the increasing use of virtual assets for money laundering and terrorist financing would help regulators around the world better co-ordinate their efforts.

"Cryptocurrency is a significant problem for AML/CTF [anti-money laundering /counter-terrorism financing] around the world and AUSTRAC in particular," Mr Jevans said.

"Regulation and enforcement around identity, know your customer, sanctions scanning and exchange of data about transactions is in the early stages.

"We expect Australia and other countries to adopt the FATF guidelines in 2020, which will help align cryptocurrency operations with those of banks and their payment network requirements.

Mr Halvorsen, chief executive of consulting firm McLean Roche, said the federal government must take money laundering more seriously.

"They need to give the laws in this area more priority and give AUSTRAC more resources to show they are taking it seriously," he said.

Mr Halvorsen said the government should look at the trust accounts operated by lawyers.

"That's a way to move illegitimate cash into a legitimate account. It's a way of laundering money," he said.

He said AUSTRAC needed more resources and tougher laws covering accountants, lawyers and real estate agents so it could counter the broad lack of compliance with anti-money laundering laws.

HEADLINE: SAVING WESTPAC THE MAVERICK ARE BANKS CRIME FIGHTERS? CHANTICLEER ANZ DODGES A BULLET SMART INVESTOR WHICH BANK? Investor's guide
David Morgan throws hat in ring
TEXT:
Chairmanship Two internal candidates among top contenders.

Westpac's former long-time chief executive David Morgan is believed to have thrown his hat in the ring to become the besieged bank's next chairman but he is likely to face opposition from some investors.

Recruiters Korn Ferry have been appointed to quickly replenish the Westpac board but bank sources say an internal candidate would be the best long-term fit.

Long-time CEO of Morgan Stanley Australia Steve Harker and former KPMG head Peter Nash are the internal front-runners; Craig Dunn is seen as too tainted from running AMP.

"We feel we've got candidates around the room," outgoing chairman Lindsay Maxsted told veteran bank analyst Brian Johnson when asked about the next chairman on a joint media and investor call. "We've got time to find the right person either for the current board to make a decision on someone there at the moment or go outside."

Mr Maxsted said the new chairman needed to come before a new CEO but governance experts are calling for a big-name external appointment and question how Mr Maxsted can be involved picking his own replacement, despite assurances that he will not.

"I struggle to see how he can be involved appointing the next CEO or chairman," one of the country's leading board recruiters said. "The first question any potential CEO wants to know is who am I working for."

The recruiter pointed to respected former Westpac and recently departed BHP and Stockland director Carolyn Hewson as an obvious option for next chairman. "She hasn't been caught in any scandal and is highly regarded."

Past Westpac directors including chairman of Virgin and IAG Elizabeth Bryan or Woolworths chairman Gordon Cairns could also be considered.

Former Westpac CEO Gail Kelly could make a remarkable return, although aside from being touted as the possible BHP chairman and sitting on the Singtel board, she has not pursued a deep career in directorship.

If the bank is pushed to appoint a chairman with less direct connections, it could look overseas to the likes of Singtel's Kiwi chairman Simon Israel.

A short-term fix could also be to consider a veteran chairman with banking experience, such as Michael Chaney or Graham Bradley, but their current commitments and age make them seem unlikely.

"David Morgan I think is a no," proxy adviser at ISS Vas Kolesnikoff said, pointing to his age, London home and short stint at BHP. "The bank has moved on from when he was there and I don't think he sends the right signal to the community and management.

A subcommittee is expected to be set up to work with Korn Ferry on the chairman's appointment but with Mr Hartzer, Mr Maxsted and director Ewen Crouch going, Mr Harker and Mr Nash candidates for the job, and more directors under threat, one investor asked: "Who is left to run it?"

The messy succession which includes Mr Maxsted staying on until next year and the debate over a new chairman means a new CEO may not be able to start until 2021.

The transition has been compared to NAB, where chairman Ken Henry stayed on long after he stood down. But in that case, the highly respected Phil Chronican was appointed acting CEO and then quickly appointed chairman-elect to pick the new CEO Ross McEwan, who starts next week.

A global search to replace Hartzer as CEO is also under way and Westpac interim chief executive Peter King is not ruling himself out.

HEADLINE: Westpac lets compliance hounds loose
TEXT:
The demoralised men and women responsible for policing their colleagues at Westpac Banking Corp - the compliance cadre - have one reason to celebrate what may emerge as the darkest regulatory stain on an Australian bank.

Westpac's shame empowers them.

With the chief executive's corpse still warm, the bank's chief risk manager, David Stephen, on Wednesday urged his hundreds of would-be crime fighters to make trouble, before trouble struck from above - in the form of another humiliating lawsuit from the regulators swarming over the industry.

For an organisation whose very existence is designed to prevent mistakes such as forgetting to send AUSTRAC 29 million financial reports, the pep talk sent an important message: we must not let this happen again.

"Now is the time to go and have those difficult conversations with the businesses," he said, according to a person present, at a previously scheduled town hall meeting at Westpac's Sydney head office.

"You are empowered to have these very difficult, very complex conversations. The voice of risk has to become stronger than ever.

"If there are any issues call them out. Even if you make mistakes, it is better to call out anything you see."

(A Westpac spokesman didn't dispute the accuracy of the comments.)

With the group collectively wondering "why isn't this fixed yet," Stephen wanted the team, which he warned would cop some of the blame for the AUSTRAC scandal, to know that, now more than ever, it is an important protector of the bank's reputation, customers and profits.

The presentation wasn't perfect. At one point Stephen used the acronym CSE, for child sexual exploitation, a reference to the pornography apparently purchased through the Westpac systems.

The phrase struck some of the compliance officers as inappropriately remote from the horror of raping children for profit - an obscene industry Westpac may have inadvertently facilitated.

A couple of days earlier, the bank demonstrated the new era of assertive compliance had arrived when it promoted a former Macquarie manager, T. Scott Saunders, to general manager for financial crime.

General manager is a big deal in Westpac. The GMs control individual businesses and report to the group heads who run the bank along with the CEO.

Saunders was hired by, and reported to, the chief compliance officer, Jamie Kelly, in April. He famously replaced the woman who admitted the breach to AUSTRAC, and managed the relationship with the regulator for 10 painful months, Amanda Wood. She was then told Westpac wanted someone more experienced.

Now, Saunders is Kelly's peer, and financial crime stands alongside credit and compliance as its own risk in need of measuring and managing.

The shift marks an evolution in structure and philosophy. Compliance was once part of Westpac's legal department, reflecting a view that it was about fulfilling the demands of the law and regulators.

Under risk, compliance became more dynamic. Its mission - which failed spectacularly - was to identify legal threats before they turned into financial costs.

Kelly and Saunders were present on Wednesday for Stephen's appearance. Perhaps in an effort to lighten the sombre mood, Kelly quipped that the scandal had been good for business at St George, a Westpac brand.

Some laughed. Others didn't.

There might be a lesson there. If compliance wants to be taken seriously across the bank, maybe the time for jokes has passed.

Key pointsWestpac's would-be crime fighters told: 'If there are

any issues call them out.'

The team has been told to have difficult conversations right across the business.

HEADLINE: Beef up systems, regulator warns
TEXT:
Following Westpac's alleged 23 million money-laundering breaches, the corporate regulator says financial services firms must step up investment in their technology systems so that harmful practices can be swiftly brought to the attention of senior managers.

Australian Securities and Investments Commission deputy chairman Karen Chester has also warned the Morrison government to avoid putting consumers at risk by succumbing to financial services "vested interests" lobbying to water down new laws in response to the banking royal commission.

In a speech to company directors in Brisbane on Friday, Ms Chester said firms that failed to adequately invest in systems and data could be exposed for sitting on "toxic revenues" that would ultimately lead to huge regulatory fines and customer remediation costs.

She put the financial sector on notice that ASIC would be "naming more names" of infringing firms so that greater transparency would increase pressure on executives and directors to improve customer protection.

Ms Chester lamented that instead of investing in compliance systems, banks and other financial services firms were spending resources on unnecessarily complex "product proliferation" for customers.

Separately on Friday, the corporate regulator and the Australian Prudential Regulation Authority signed an updated memorandum of understanding in response to the Hayne inquiry's recommendation.
